title: 50 Python Practice Problems: Orders and Customers Drills
summary: Fifty solved Python 3.11+ drills over one shared orders/customers dataset, from comprehensions and sorting through grouping, strings, itertools, closures, generators and error handling to interview-style problems.

chapters.title: 50 Python Drills: Orders and Customers
points: Comprehensions and filtering: Q1-Q6
Sorting with keys: Q7-Q11
Grouping with dict, defaultdict and Counter: Q12-Q17
String processing: Q18-Q22
itertools: Q23-Q28
Functions and closures: Q29-Q33
Generators: Q34-Q39
Error handling: Q40-Q44
Interview problems (top-k, dedupe, sliding window): Q45-Q50

chapters.title: The Shared Dataset
points: customers is a list of 6 dicts with keys id, name, city, tier, email. Ids run 1-6 and customer 6 (Fay Ono) has no orders.
orders is a list of 8 dicts with keys id, customer_id, amount, status, category, date, qty. Ids run 101-108, statuses are paid, refunded, pending and cancelled, and dates are ISO strings.
Every drill uses these two lists exactly as given: ids are ints, amounts are floats, and the code targets Python 3.11+ with imports shown inside each solution.
Shared helper used in many drills: names = {c['id']: c['name'] for c in customers} maps a customer id to a name.

chapters.title: Comprehensions and Filtering
points: Q1. List the ids of paid orders. Code: [o['id'] for o in orders if o['status'] == 'paid']. Result: [101, 102, 104, 106, 107]
Q2. Uppercase the names of gold customers. Code: [c['name'].upper() for c in customers if c['tier'] == 'gold']. Result: ['ASHA RAO', 'CHEN LI']
Q3. Build an id-to-amount dict for orders of 100 or more. Code: {o['id']: o['amount'] for o in orders if o['amount'] >= 100}. Result: {101: 250.0, 103: 120.0, 104: 300.0, 106: 150.0}
Q4. Get the distinct categories as a sorted list. Code: sorted({o['category'] for o in orders}). Result: ['books', 'games', 'toys']
Q5. List paid orders with amount over 100. Code: [o['id'] for o in orders if o['amount'] > 100 and o['status'] == 'paid']. Result: [101, 104, 106]

Q6. Pair each paid order id with its customer name. Code: [(o['id'], names[o['customer_id']]) for o in orders if o['status'] == 'paid']. Result: [(101, 'Asha Rao'), (102, 'Ben Cole'), (104, 'Chen Li'), (106, 'Chen Li'), (107, 'Ben Cole')]

chapters.title: Sorting with Keys
points: Q7. Sort order ids by amount, highest first. Code: [o['id'] for o in sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o['amount'], reverse=True)]. Result: [104, 101, 106, 103, 102, 107, 108, 105] (the 80.0 tie keeps 102 before 107 because sorted is stable)

Q8. Sort customers by tier (gold, silver, bronze), then by name. Code: rank = {'gold': 0, 'silver': 1, 'bronze': 2}; [c['name'] for c in sorted(customers, key=lambda c: (rank[c['tier']], c['name']))]. Result: ['Asha Rao', 'Chen Li', 'Ben Cole', 'Eli Park', 'Dara Singh', 'Fay Ono']

Q9. Sort order ids by category ascending, then amount descending. Code: [o['id'] for o in sorted(orders, key=lambda o: (o['category'], -o['amount']))]. Result: [104, 101, 107, 106, 103, 102, 108, 105]
Q10. Find the two customers with the longest names. Code: [c['name'] for c in sorted(customers, key=lambda c: len(c['name']), reverse=True)[:2]]. Result: ['Dara Singh', 'Asha Rao']
Q11. Find the cheapest and the priciest order ids with min and max. Code: (min(orders, key=lambda o: o['amount'])['id'], max(orders, key=lambda o: o['amount'])['id']). Result: (105, 104)

chapters.title: Grouping with dict, defaultdict and Counter
points: Q12. Count orders per customer id with defaultdict(int). Code: from collections import defaultdict; d = defaultdict(int); [d.__setitem__(o['customer_id'], d[o['customer_id']] + 1) for o in orders]; dict(d). Result: {1: 2, 2: 2, 3: 2, 4: 1, 5: 1}

Q13. Group order ids by status with defaultdict(list). Code: g = defaultdict(list); for o in orders: g[o['status']].append(o['id']); dict(g). Result: {'paid': [101, 102, 104, 106, 107], 'refunded': [103], 'pending': [105], 'cancelled': [108]}

Q14. Total the paid amount per category. Code: t = defaultdict(float); for o in orders: if o['status'] == 'paid': t[o['category']] += o['amount']; dict(t). Result: {'books': 630.0, 'toys': 80.0, 'games': 150.0}

Q15. Count how many orders have each status with Counter. Code: from collections import Counter; Counter(o['status'] for o in orders). Result: Counter({'paid': 5, 'refunded': 1, 'pending': 1, 'cancelled': 1})

Q16. Total the units sold per category over paid orders, with Counter. Code: u = Counter(); for o in orders: if o['status'] == 'paid': u[o['category']] += o['qty']; u. Result: Counter({'books': 6, 'games': 2, 'toys': 1})

Q17. Find the average paid amount per customer. Code: p = defaultdict(list); for o in orders: if o['status'] == 'paid': p[o['customer_id']].append(o['amount']); {k: sum(v) / len(v) for k, v in p.items()}. Result: {1: 250.0, 2: 80.0, 3: 225.0}

chapters.title: String Processing
points: Q18. Count the customers per email domain. Code: from collections import Counter; dict(Counter(c['email'].split('@')[1] for c in customers)). Result: {'shop.io': 3, 'mail.com': 3}
Q19. Build initials from each name. Code: [''.join(w[0] for w in c['name'].split()) for c in customers]. Result: ['AR', 'BC', 'CL', 'DS', 'EP', 'FO']
Q20. Turn each name into a lowercase slug. Code: ['-'.join(c['name'].lower().split()) for c in customers]. Result: ['asha-rao', 'ben-cole', 'chen-li', 'dara-singh', 'eli-park', 'fay-ono']
Q21. Format order 101 as an aligned receipt line. Code: o = orders[0]; i, cat, amt = o['id'], o['category'], o['amount']; f'#{i:>4} {cat:<6} {amt:8.2f}'. Result: '# 101 books    250.00'

Q22. Mask the local part of each email. Code: [e[0] + '***@' + e.split('@')[1] for e in (c['email'] for c in customers)]. Result: ['a***@shop.io', 'b***@mail.com', 'c***@shop.io', 'd***@mail.com', 'e***@shop.io', 'f***@mail.com']

chapters.title: itertools
points: Q23. Build the running total of paid amounts with accumulate. Code: from itertools import accumulate; list(accumulate(o['amount'] for o in orders if o['status'] == 'paid')). Result: [250.0, 330.0, 630.0, 780.0, 860.0]

Q24. Sum qty per category with groupby (sort by the key first). Code: from itertools import groupby; s = sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o['category']); {k: sum(o['qty'] for o in g) for k, g in groupby(s, key=lambda o: o['category'])}. Result: {'books': 6, 'games': 3, 'toys': 3}

Q25. Find pairs of customers who live in the same city, using combinations. Code: from itertools import combinations; [(a['name'], b['name']) for a, b in combinations(customers, 2) if a['city'] == b['city']]. Result: [('Asha Rao', 'Dara Singh'), ('Ben Cole', 'Chen Li'), ('Eli Park', 'Fay Ono')]

Q26. Build a tier by status grid with product. Code: from itertools import product; list(product(['gold', 'silver'], ['paid', 'refunded'])). Result: [('gold', 'paid'), ('gold', 'refunded'), ('silver', 'paid'), ('silver', 'refunded')]

Q27. Join the paid and the refunded order ids into one sequence with chain. Code: from itertools import chain; list(chain([o['id'] for o in orders if o['status'] == 'paid'], [o['id'] for o in orders if o['status'] == 'refunded'])). Result: [101, 102, 104, 106, 107, 103]

Q28. Find the longest streak of consecutive paid orders with groupby on the raw order. Code: from itertools import groupby; max(len(list(g)) for k, g in groupby(orders, key=lambda o: o['status']) if k == 'paid'). Result: 2

chapters.title: Functions and Closures
points: Q29. Write a total with a keyword-only status that defaults to paid. Code: def total(rows, *, status='paid'): return sum(o['amount'] for o in rows if o['status'] == status). Result: total(orders) -> 860.0 and total(orders, status='refunded') -> 120.0
Q30. Build a filter factory with a closure. Code: def by_status(s): return lambda o: o['status'] == s; paid = by_status('paid'); len(list(filter(paid, orders))). Result: 5
Q31. Build a call counter with nonlocal. Code: def counter(): n = 0; def inc(): nonlocal n; n += 1; return n; return inc; c = counter(); [c(), c(), c()]. Result: [1, 2, 3]

Q32. Spot and fix the late-binding closure bug. Code: fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; [f() for f in fs] returns [2, 2, 2]; the fix fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)] returns [0, 1, 2]. Result: [2, 2, 2] before, [0, 1, 2] after

Q33. Apply a 10 percent discount with functools.partial. Code: from functools import partial; def scale(x, rate): return round(x * rate, 2); disc = partial(scale, rate=0.9); [disc(o['amount']) for o in orders[:3]]. Result: [225.0, 72.0, 108.0]

chapters.title: Generators
points: Q34. Yield paid order ids lazily with a generator function. Code: def paid_ids(rows): for o in rows: if o['status'] == 'paid': yield o['id']; list(paid_ids(orders)). Result: [101, 102, 104, 106, 107]
Q35. Sum paid amounts with a generator expression, no intermediate list. Code: sum(o['amount'] for o in orders if o['status'] == 'paid'). Result: 860.0

Q36. Process orders in chunks of 3 with a generator. Code: def chunks(seq, n): for i in range(0, len(seq), n): yield seq[i:i + n]; [[o['id'] for o in ch] for ch in chunks(orders, 3)]. Result: [[101, 102, 103], [104, 105, 106], [107, 108]]

Q37. Take the first match with next and a default. Code: next((o['id'] for o in orders if o['amount'] > 200), None) gives 101; next((o['id'] for o in orders if o['amount'] > 500), None) gives None. Result: 101 and None

Q38. Stream a 3-order moving average with a generator and deque(maxlen=3). Code: from collections import deque; def moving_avg(rows, k=3): w = deque(maxlen=k); for o in rows: w.append(o['amount']); if len(w) == k: yield round(sum(w) / k, 2); list(moving_avg(orders)). Result: [150.0, 166.67, 155.0, 165.0, 91.67, 96.67]

Q39. Yield the names of customers with no orders, lazily. Code: def idle(cs, os): ordered = {o['customer_id'] for o in os}; for c in cs: if c['id'] not in ordered: yield c['name']; list(idle(customers, orders)). Result: ['Fay Ono']

chapters.title: Error Handling
points: Q40. Return 'unknown' for a missing customer id with try/except KeyError. Code: def name_of(cid): try: return names[cid] except KeyError: return 'unknown'. Result: name_of(3) -> 'Chen Li', name_of(9) -> 'unknown'
Q41. Parse amount strings and skip bad ones with ValueError. Code: out = []; for x in ['250', 'abc', '80.5']: try: out.append(float(x)) except ValueError: pass; out. Result: [250.0, 80.5]

Q42. Raise and catch a custom exception. Code: class InvalidOrder(Exception): pass; def check(o): if o['amount'] <= 0: raise InvalidOrder(f'order {o["id"]} has amount {o["amount"]}'); try: check({'id': 9, 'amount': -5}) except InvalidOrder as e: str(e). Result: 'order 9 has amount -5'

Q43. Average a customer's order amounts, returning 0.0 when there are none. Code: def avg(xs): try: return sum(xs) / len(xs) except ZeroDivisionError: return 0.0. Result: avg([80.0, 80.0]) -> 80.0 and avg([]) -> 0.0

Q44. Total paid spend per customer, using dict.get with a default so missing customers give 0.0 instead of KeyError. Code: spend = {}; for o in orders: if o['status'] == 'paid': spend[o['customer_id']] = spend.get(o['customer_id'], 0.0) + o['amount']; [(c['name'], spend.get(c['id'], 0.0)) for c in customers]. Result: [('Asha Rao', 250.0), ('Ben Cole', 160.0), ('Chen Li', 450.0), ('Dara Singh', 0.0), ('Eli Park', 0.0), ('Fay Ono', 0.0)]

chapters.title: Interview Problems: Top-k, Dedupe, Sliding Window
points: Q45. Find the top 3 orders by amount with heapq.nlargest. Code: from heapq import nlargest; [o['id'] for o in nlargest(3, orders, key=lambda o: o['amount'])]. Result: [104, 101, 106]

Q46. Find the customer with the highest paid spend. Code: from collections import Counter; spend = Counter(); for o in orders: if o['status'] == 'paid': spend[o['customer_id']] += o['amount']; names[max(spend, key=spend.get)]. Result: 'Chen Li' (spend is 250.0, 160.0 and 450.0 for customers 1, 2 and 3)
Q47. Dedupe categories while keeping first-seen order. Code: list(dict.fromkeys(o['category'] for o in orders)). Result: ['books', 'toys', 'games']

Q48. Keep only the first order of each customer. Code: seen = set(); out = []; for o in orders: if o['customer_id'] not in seen: seen.add(o['customer_id']); out.append(o['id']); out. Result: [101, 102, 104, 105, 108]

Q49. Two-sum: find two orders whose amounts add up to 330. Code: seen = {}; for o in orders: need = 330 - o['amount']; if need in seen: pair = (seen[need], o['id']); break; seen[o['amount']] = o['id']; pair. Result: (101, 102)

Q50. Find the best sum of any 3 consecutive order amounts with a sliding window. Code: a = [o['amount'] for o in orders]; s = sum(a[:3]); best = s; for i in range(3, len(a)): s += a[i] - a[i - 3]; best = max(best, s); best. Result: 500.0 (orders 102, 103, 104)

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Python Drill Idioms
points: Comprehensions: [x for x in xs if cond], {k: v for ...}, {x for ...}; a generator expression in sum() or max() avoids building a list.
Sorting: sorted(xs, key=...) is stable; use a tuple key for multi-level order and negate a number for descending on that part; min and max take key too.
Grouping: defaultdict(list) to collect, defaultdict(int or float) to total, Counter for counts and most_common, dict.fromkeys(xs) to dedupe in order.
itertools: accumulate for running totals, groupby only after sorting by the same key, combinations for pairs, product for grids, chain to join.
Closures and generators: nonlocal rebinds an outer name, lambda i=i fixes late binding, yield makes a lazy sequence, next(it, default) avoids StopIteration.
Interviews: heapq.nlargest for top-k, a set or dict for O(1) lookups (dedupe, two-sum), and a running window sum or deque(maxlen=k) for sliding windows in O(n).
